items.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002
items.q: He was kind of a spiritual and artistic father to me... he championed me and taught me a lot.

ctx.x: Let me throw a couple names at you and see just your recollections. Lou Donaldson?

He was kind of a spiritual and artistic father to me. I met him the same way I met Charlie Rouse. Well first of all before I left home Torrie Zito was working in the strip joints and all that and writing arrangements for some of the acts in those strip joints in Rome and Utica, and made good money, and would buy up all of the latest Blue Note records and whatever, Verve records. He’d order them from New York, mostly because you couldn’t get them in Utica too much. And so I’d go to visit Ronnie and Ronnie and I…

he was but I never tried to introduce myself or anything. I don’t think we did that in those days. But he came up to me and asked me to work with him. I think that was after Rouse asked me to work with him. Yeah it was after, because I remember I didn’t have a local musician’s union card. And to get one you had to transfer from your home town local, put in a formal, what they called a transfer. items.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jimmy Wormworth was the drummer. We went up to Buffalo, and hit some of the same clubs.

ctx.x: So by the time you’d made those first records, you’d been working with him for a year or more.
Yeah. Herman Foster, Peck. Morrison, and Jimmy Wormworth was the drummer. We went up to Buffalo, and hit some of the same clubs. But we had it set up...
That’s when you started establishing that circuit and those relationships.
